blocks.title: Condensation Polymerisation
blocks.text: In condensation polymerisation, monomers join together, but each time a new bond forms, a small molecule is eliminated from the monomers.

This small molecule is usually water can also be H₂O, HCl or CH₃OH, or NH₃. Monomers must have at least two reactive functional groups (like -OH, -COOH, -NH₂) that can react with each other. These groups are on different ends of the monomer(s). Small molecules are always produced as a side product. This typically happens in a "step-by-step" manner as depicted in Figure 26.3.

blocks.alt: Condensation polymerisation: monomers H-X-H and HO-Y-OH, 'Monomers of two types'. They line up as H-X-[H+HO]-Y-[OH+H]-X-[H+HO]-Y-OH, the H and OH at each join in dashed boxes. A yellow arrow labelled 'Condensation reaction' leads to H-X-Y-X-Y-OH + 3H2O.
blocks.caption: Figure 26.3: Illustration of condensation polymerisation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 26.3).

blocks.text: Polyesters have ester links [—C(=O)—O—] in their backbone. A diol (molecule with two -OH groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (molecule with two -COOH groups) as monomers are combined to give polyester. The -OH from the diol reacts with the -COOH from the acid. A molecule of water is removed as shown below.

blocks.alt: Monomers: HOCH2CH2OH (ethane-1,2-diol) and HOOC-C6H4-COOH (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid). Polymerisation: ...+ HOCH2CH2OH HOOC-C6H4-COOH HOCH2CH2OH HOOC-C6H4-COOH +..., with the H of each diol OH and the OH of each acid group in magenta. An arrow leads to ...OCH2CH2OOC-C6H4-COOCH2CH2OOC-C6H4-CO-..., with + H2O under each of the four ester links.
blocks.caption: Preparation of Terylene/PET, a polyester from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 148).

blocks.text: Polyesters have special features, such as high tensile strength, which make them suitable to manufacture fibres. Polyester is used as an alternative to cotton due to its low cost and ability to resist creases. It is also used as a plastic; for example, PETE is used in making plastic bottles for beverages and other food packaging. Polyester is also used as cross links to obtain hard plastics. An example is the glass fibre reinforced cross-linked polyester.
Polyamides have amide links [—C(=O)—NH—] in their backbone. They can be prepared from many starting materials.
i) From a Diamine and a Dicarboxylic Acid

A diamine (molecule with two -NH₂ groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (molecule with two -COOH groups) are joined together to give polyamide. The -NH₂ from the diamine reacts with the -COOH from the acid. A molecule of water is removed.

blocks.alt: nH2N-CH2-NH2 (diamine) + nHOOC-CH2-COOH (dicarboxylic acid) gives [-HN-CH2-NH-C(=O)-CH2-C(=O)-]n (polyamide) + 2nH2O, with each C=O drawn as O above C.
blocks.caption: Polyamide from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 149).

blocks.text: Example: Nylon 6,6 uses hexamethylenediamine and Adipic acid.
ii) From a Diamine and a Dioyl Chloride

A diamine and a dioyl chloride (molecule with two -COCl groups) as monomers are joined to give polyamide. Dioyl chlorides are more reactive than dicarboxylic acids. The -NH₂ from the diamine reacts with the -COCl from the dioyl chloride. A molecule of hydrogen chloride (HCl) is removed. General equation is given below:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed schemes give + nH₂O (diamine and dicarboxylic acid) and + nHCl (diamine and dioyl chloride). Each repeat unit has two amide links and each link releases one small molecule, so the figures show + 2nH₂O and + 2nHCl. In the amino-acid scheme each unit has one link, so + nH₂O is right.

An amino acid is a single monomer that has both an -NH₂ (amino) group and a -COOH (carboxylic acid) group in one molecule. The -NH₂ group of one amino acid reacts with the -COOH group of another amino acid removing a water to form a peptide bond. Peptide bond is also a type of amide linkage. General equation is given below:

blocks.caption: Polyamide (polypeptide) from an amino acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 149).

blocks.text: Proteins are natural polyamides made from amino acids, which will be discussed in Biochemistry (Chapter 27).

Amide linkage is also formed between acyl chlorides, a very reactive organic compound and an amine, e.g. ammonia. methanamine (CH₃-NH₂), N, N-dimethylamine, (CH₃)₂NH. When an acyl chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine, a molecule of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas is removed. This reaction happens easily at room temperature because acyl chlorides are fairly reactive.

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-Cl (acyl chloride) + R'-NH2 (amine) gives R-C(=O)-NH-R' (amide) + HCl (hydrogen chloride).
blocks.caption: Amide from an acyl chloride and an amine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 149).
